episodes.research_focus: Fictional local fiscal archive; Suetonius on Domitianic enforcement and Dio on Nerva.

claims.claim: Suetonius reports rigorous enforcement under Domitian and recalls a public examination of a 90-year-old man.
claims.caveat: Does not establish universal practice, tax creation by Domitian, or abolition by Nerva.

claims.claim: Dio 68.1.2 says Nerva prohibited accusations of maiestas or adopting the Jewish mode of life.
claims.caveat: Does not state that the fiscus itself was abolished.

constraints: The selected96CE date is editorial; the fiscal archive, reconciliation task and Rome–Ostia journey are fictional unless independently established.
Berlin specimenRICII82 is dated97CE; do not present it as an object minted in96 or knowledge available to a96scene. OCRE58 remains unverified.
Dio and fiscal legend do not demonstrate abolition of the tax. Distinguish relief from accusations/enforcement from cancellation of every liability.
No surveyed archive building, ancient road alignment, port phase or playable area is established here.

episodes.research_focus: Witness tradition with competing rabbinic attributions.

claims.claim: Mishnah RH 1:6 attributes the detention of more than forty pairs to Rabbi Akiva.
claims.caveat: Not contemporaneous verification; date and reported number are not independently established.

claims.claim: Bavli RH 22a, in a baraita attributed to Rabbi Yehuda, rejects Akiva and names Zefer, head of Geder.
claims.caveat: Transliteration varies (Zefer/Shazpar). Neither attribution should be presented as settled contemporary fact.

constraints: The selected c100–135CE band is an editorial envelope, not a date supplied byRH1.6 or22a.

The accessed English translation adds explanatory itinerary/destination wording. It cannot establish an early2ndcentury route to Jerusalem or a parcel atLod. Separate later tradition, translator gloss and period-specific geography.
Keep Akiva attribution and RabbiYehuda alternative naming Zefer(headGeder) distinct; do not turn either into an uncontested eyewitness fact.
No academy location, school footprint, road/river crossing or timed teaching escort is established by these passages.

episodes.research_focus: Local reconstruction of civilian refuge during revolt.

claims.claim: Dio 68.32 describes revolt in Cyrene and names Andreas as leader.
claims.caveat: Hostile literary framing and very large death tolls are not independently verified.

claims.claim: Eusebius HE 4.2 describes events in Cyrene and names Lucuas.
claims.caveat: Different leader/frame than Dio; preserve source distinction.

constraints: Dio and Eusebius are distinct retrospective transmissions; neither provides a neutral event log or verified casualty census.
Do not equate Andreas andLucuas without an explicit qualified argument; do not merge hostile atrocity rhetoric with objective collection narration.
Individual households, relief parties, witness notes and supply operations remain fictional; these passages do not attest those groups or identify their destinations.
Exact ancient refuge/harbour layout, dated coast, water access, terrain routes and scenario clock still require archaeological and geographic evidence.

episodes.research_focus: Local Egyptian reconstruction; distinguish reports and avoid generalized culpability.

claims.claim: Dio 68.32 reports violence in Egypt and Cyprus during the revolt.
claims.caveat: Do not transfer all claims about Cyrene to Alexandria or treat casualty totals as census.

claims.claim: Eusebius HE 4.2 reports revolt in Alexandria/Egypt and Cyrene and Roman suppression.
claims.caveat: Not eyewitness testimony; do not merge with Dio as a single certain account.

constraints: Dio and Eusebius are distinct retrospective transmissions; neither provides a neutral event log or verified casualty census.
Do not equate Andreas andLucuas without an explicit qualified argument; do not merge hostile atrocity rhetoric with objective collection narration.
Individual households, relief parties, witness notes and supply operations remain fictional; these passages do not attest those groups or identify their destinations.
Exact ancient refuge/harbour layout, dated coast, water access, terrain routes and scenario clock still require archaeological and geographic evidence.
Eusebius distinguishes violence inAlexandria and forces fromCyrene intoEgypt; a regional report is not evidence for a specific harbour encounter.
